I worked as a graphic designer, screen printer, and offset pressman right out of high school for a handful of years.

Before buying any fabric that has been screen printed (this especially applies to t-shirts and hoodies as they get washed the most often) always stretch a small corner of the graphic and try to pull it apart. If you are able to pull the ink apart and see shirt threads through the design then either the print was not inked heavily enough or it has not been cured at a high enough temperature. In both cases the shirts will begin cracking and washing out the design well before you get them through a dozen washes.
Before buying any graphic printed t-shirt/hoodie/pant etc.

No problem, this especially applies to department stores like walmart, pennies, whatever. I think about a third of the shirts I've done this too at these stores has failed this test.

It's a big enough issue, quality control wise, that if more than two shirts randomly selected failed the stretch test at the print shop I worked at we'd run them through the curer again. Big manufactures though don't have time for this usually so more low quality prints get through.

I do self printing for fun. I noticed some of these when laying ink. Then I started doing it heavy handed. Yet, I just use a hair dryer to cure the ink. Do you think that will get it hot enough? I wash them hot after normally to check them.

Ink needs to reach a temperature somewhere between 300 and 400 degrees for a dozen or so seconds before it is cured completely. The hair dryer may be curing the top layer but I doubt it would do a very good job.

For hobby printing I don't think you need to spend the 1000+ dollars on a conveyor dryer, I do think you should look into getting a flash dryer though. Something like that or even cheaper if you can find it. Using a flash dryer and one of those infrared temp guns you should be able to tell when a print is cured enough. Though a flash dryer is never going to cure it as well as a conveyor one it will definitely get the job done for what you're trying.

It is super easy to burn shirts with flash dryers though, and there main function is to semi-cure ink quickly but not totally so you can print additional colors on top of the semi-cured ink and not risk blurring or sticking like you would with wet ink (which would happen if you didn't use enough spray adhesive to keep the shirt in place or if the colors were off register from each other). If you get a flash adjust it to be higher than normal and experiment with it until it cures ink reliably without burning shirts, itll take some work but I hope that helps!

How many arms does your press have and do you do a lot of multi color jobs?

It's been a while for sure for me, so I'm basing this on memories that more than 5 years old lol, but in general the less detailed the design the lower the mesh count you want and the mesh material matters. For an image that is just a bold type style I'd use an 80 or 100/110 mesh screen. The bigger the mesh the easier it is to pull essentially and the more ink coverage you get so you don't have to do multiple pulls to get the right amount of brightness and coverage. On one or two color images that have a halftone I'd use something 150+ mesh count. If you're trying to print an image in CMYK I'd get 4 200+ silk mesh screens to do those jobs on as that is a very very very fine half-tone you'd be printing and make your ink thin.

This kind of leads into your next question as well. Get some ink thinner if you don't, the more detailed the job the higher the mesh needs to be and the thinner your ink needs to be. The thinner your ink is the harder your squeegee needs to be. Soft squeegees work well for thick inks (usually white, I don't know why off the top of my head but white is always super think and it needs a lot of thinning for detailed jobs) and harder squeegees work better on thinned ink. Regardless of ink thickness and squeegee hardness you want to keep your pulls consistent in the pressure applied department and the angle of your squeegee. If you keep pressure and angle good and the same for all jobs then you only need to change squeegees depending on the ink properties. This will really help if you move into doing CMYK jobs because if you pull your black at a different angle than your Cyan your colors will look off.

This is very important news. The interest you pay on your debt is a direct drag on the funds available to provide services to the country. A government will always have some debt, because it is more productive to operate necessary funding requirements with low interest debt than to operate those same functions from cash surpluses - when the economy is growing faster than the interest rate on the debt.

If your economy is growing it is best to have all of your cash invested in that growth... it's value increases faster than the interest penalty incurred on loans. Thus you maximize your possible returns.

Now if the total bill you pay in interest expenses is growing at a slower rate each year than the country's GDP, the net burden of financing the country is decreasing - while the available funds to service growth, as a percentage of your total wealth, is increasing.

This means, your total debt CAN increase each year, so long as the interest on that debt is growing more slowly than the country itself. Even as your debt is increasing, the burden of that debt is decreasing... and that is the critical part you are trying to achieve.

Side Note: In the history of modern national debt financing, when debt reaches about 100% of GDP is usually when governments take stronger measures to get the growth of their debt under control, in part because that is when the bond markets start to look more closely at your credit ratings. Debt at 50% of GDP is considered very healthy. Debt at 150% is considered quite troubling.
